item.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
item.description: arXiv:2610.28930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $\Delta$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrt\Delta,n^2/\Delta\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+n\tau+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $\tau$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.
item.dc:creator: Qin Xin

item.title: Solving problems in RDV Graphs faster and easier
item.description: arXiv:2610.28932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In interval graphs and many generalizations thereof, problems such as Matching, Independent Set, and Dominating Set can be solved with simple greedy algorithms in linear (i.e., $O(m+n)$) time. However, it is sometimes possible to improve on this runtime if a suitable representation as intersection graph is given; for example it is possible to find a minimum dominating set in an interval graph in $O(n)$ time. We study RDV graphs, a generalization of interval graphs, namely, the intersection graphs of directed paths in a rooted tree. It was known that the above three problems can be solved in $O(n\log n)$ time if a suitably small representation is given. In this paper, we reduce the runtime to $O(n)$. Furthermore, while the previous results used non-trivial operations such as range-minimum queries and ray-shooting queries, we need nothing more complicated than lists and (for Matching) a Union-Find data structure.
item.dc:creator: Therese Biedl, G\"unter Rote

item.title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Bounds for Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2610.29037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of characterizing the optimal consistency--robustness tradeoff for single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predicted processing times. For a fixed number of jobs $n$, Wei and Zhang (2020) established a lower bound on the achievable consistency--robustness tradeoff which is known to be tight only in a few restrictive cases, leaving the optimal tradeoff for general $n$ unresolved. A different worst-case-$n$ regime was introduced by Benomar et al. (2025), who applied the former work's construction to show that for $\lambda \in (0, 1)$, any $(1+\lambda)$-consistent algorithm must be $1 + \Omega(\sqrt{1/\lambda})$-robust. On the other hand, the best known upper bound gives $(1+\lambda)$-consistency and $1+O(1/\lambda)$-robustness, leaving a polynomial gap. In this work, we develop a new lower bound using a multi-stage adversarial construction and a new algorithm that together give a near-optimal characterization of the consistency--robustness tradeoff: for every $n$, our upper bound is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of our lower bound, and thus our algorithm is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of the online optimal. In particular, our lower bound shows that any $(1+\lambda)$-consistent algorithm must have robustness at least $1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ as $n \to \infty$, while our algorithm achieves robustness at most $\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}+1/\lambda}$ for any $n$, matching the lower bound in the leading term as $\lambda \downarrow 0$; our upper bound also closes the polynomial gap in the worst-case-$n$ regime. We additionally show how our algorithm can be made error-tolerant, preserving the near-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff while incurring only slightly degraded performance under bounded prediction errors.
item.dc:creator: Sizhe Li, Nicolas Christianson, Tongxin Li

item.title: Optimal Labeling Schemes for $\Gamma$-Free Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.29184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study labeling schemes for $p \times q$ $\Gamma$-free binary matrices, which do not contain a submatrix of the form $\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. We give a labeling scheme that uses $O(\log^2 N)$-bit labels for rows and columns, where $N=p+q$, such that any matrix entry can be determined from the corresponding two labels in constant time in the word RAM model. The worst-case label size matches the counting lower bound up to constant factors. We also show that the entrywise least $\Gamma$-free supermatrix of an arbitrary $p\times q$ binary matrix, together with its labels, can be constructed in $O(pq)$ time. Our construction represents a $\Gamma$-free matrix by a sequence of rooted forests, where each column corresponds to a node and the $1$-entries of each row form a root path in its corresponding forest. For $n$-vertex strongly chordal and chordal bipartite graphs, our result gives asymptotically optimal $O(\log^2 n)$-bit adjacency labeling schemes with constant-time queries. These results answer both representation questions posed by Spinrad in 1995.
item.dc:creator: Sankardeep Chakraborty, Seungbum Jo

item.title: On the Largest Cardinality Subset Sum
item.description: arXiv:2610.29280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Largest Cardinality Subset Sum (LCSS): given $n$ nonnegative integers and a target $t$, compute a subset summing to $t$ with maximum cardinality. We also consider its all-targets version (ATLCSS), which asks for this maximum for every sum $s\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. The LCSS problem sits squarely between the subset sum and the knapsack problem. A straightforward dynamic-programming algorithm runs in time $O(nt)$ and solves ATLCSS, and using Jin and Bringmann (both in STOC 2024, independent work) $0$-$1$ knapsack results we achieve a $\widetilde{O}(n + a_{\max}^2)$-time deterministic algorithm for LCSS. Our main result is a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+\sqrt{n}\,t)$-time algorithm for LCSS. Then, we complement this result with a randomized $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$-time algorithm for ATLCSS. Together, our two algorithms give a $\widetilde{O}(n+t\min\{\sqrt{n},\sqrt{t}\})$-time algorithm for LCSS. As an application of ATLCSS, we solve the search version of Projection Subset Sum, introduced by Dutta and Rajasree (SYNSAC 2023), in $\widetilde{O}(n+t^{3/2})$ time for every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $p\geq 1$. For $\ell_1$, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n+t)$ time, removing the unique-representation assumption required by their algorithm. Both algorithms output an optimal modified vector and a witnessing subset.
item.dc:creator: Deepak Bhati, Anubhav Dhar, Pranjal Dutta, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree, Karol W\k{e}grzycki

item.title: How to Walk a Dog in Parallel: On Parallel Computation of the Discrete Frechet Distance
item.description: arXiv:2610.29296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Fr\'echet distance (also known as the dog-leash distance) is a well-studied and prevalent distance measure for polygonal curves. In this paper we present parallel algorithms for computing the discrete \frechet\ distance between two curves, in both the PRAM and MPC models. For two polygonal curves of length $n$, we show that the distance between them can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log n/ \sigma)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+\sigma})$ total work for any $0<\sigma<1$. In the sublinear MPC model with $n^\rho$ space per machine, it can be computed in $O(\log n / \rho^2)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{2+\rho})$ total space. For $c$-packed curves, we match our bounds to the sequential algorithms, showing that a $(1+\eps)$-approximation of the distance can be computed in the PRAM model in $O(\log{n}+1/\sigma^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+\sigma})$ total work, and in the sublinear MPC model in $O(1 /\rho^3)$ rounds and $\tilde{O}(n^{1+\rho})$ total space, for any constant $\eps>0$. As part of our algorithms for $c$-packed curves, we also present parallel algorithms for computing curve simplifications, which may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Leonid Barenboim, Arnold Filtser, Omrit Filtser, Orr Fischer

item.title: Dynamically optimal weight-balanced binary search trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.29574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In STOC 1972, J{\"{u}}rg Nievergelt and Edward M.~Reingold introduced the $BB[\alpha]$-tree, also known as a \emph{weight-balanced} tree, which for any $\alpha \in (0,\frac{1}{2}]$ is a binary search tree where every node with induced subtree size $s$ has children with induced subtree sizes at least $\alpha(s+1)-1$. A new rotation-based binary search tree, the \emph{PopTree}, is introduced. The PopTree stores $n$ elements and is a $BB[\tfrac1{20}]$-tree after the execution of each search and a $BB[\tfrac1{729}]$-tree at all times, notably while rebalancing. For any constant $\alpha$, its performance on search sequences of length $\Omega(n \log n)$ is proved to be within a constant factor (which can depend on $\alpha$) of the optimal offline rotation-based binary search tree that maintains the $BB[\alpha]$ balance invariant.
item.dc:creator: John Iacono, Akash Pareek

item.title: Tight Space Bounds for Pivot-Based Distance Oracles in Sparse Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An approximate distance oracle (ADO) is a compact data structure that answers distance queries within a multiplicative \emph{stretch} $k$. The classical oracle of Thorup and Zwick~[STOC'01, JACM'05] has stretch $k=2\ell-1$ and uses $O(\ell n^{1+1/\ell})$ space, for every integer $\ell\ge1$, and this trade-off is optimal for dense graphs under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture. However, for sparse graphs ($m=O(n)$), their lower bound yields nothing beyond $\Omega(m)$ space. A pivot-based $1$-hop ADO gives every vertex $\tilde{O}(1)$ pivots and returns as an estimate the length of a walk of the form $u\to p_u \to p_v \to v$, where $p_u$ is a pivot of $u$, $p_v$ is a pivot of $v$, and $p_u\to p_v$ is a stored distance. We observe that all the state-of-the-art ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time are in fact pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs. Our main result is that, under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture for graphs with constant degree, there are sparse graphs on which every \emph{pivot-based} $1$-hop ADO with stretch $k$ requires $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(k+1)})$ space, for every \emph{real} $k\ge1$. This matches the best known upper bounds with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time, up to polylogarithmic factors, at every stretch where they are known. We also extend our lower bound to pivot-based ADOs with any constant number $\beta$ of hops, showing that they require $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(\beta(k+1))})$ space. In addition, we obtain a tight lower bound for two-hop hopsets. Under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture, for every integer $\ell\ge3$, $(2\ell-3,2)$-hopsets on sparse graphs require size $\Omega(m^{1+1/\ell})$, which matches a construction based on the oracles of [Kadria and Roditty, ISAAC'25]. Using the recent explicit high-girth graphs of Double Agent~[doubleAI'26], we also obtain unconditional versions of our ADO lower bounds, with the exponent above $1$ multiplied by $4/5$.
item.dc:creator: Avi Kadria, Liam Roditty

item.title: Fully Dynamic Triangle and 4-Vertex Subgraph Counting: From Theory to Practice and Back Again
item.description: arXiv:2610.29776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counting small patterns is a core primitive in large-scale graph analytics, with numerous applications in data management and network analysis. As modern graphs are massive and continuously evolving, maintaining such counts efficiently under updates is essential. Although specialized dynamic algorithms for patterns with up to four vertices exist, they remain largely theoretical; practitioners instead rely on general-purpose or approximate methods. We present an in-depth study of two dynamic approaches by Eppstein et al. and Hanauer et al. for maintaining counts of triangles and all connected four-vertex subgraph patterns, both based on variants of heavy-light vertex partitioning. We introduce theoretical and practical optimizations and develop hybrid variants that combine complementary strengths of both approaches. Experiments on 56 large real-world and synthetic dynamic graphs show that our optimized algorithms outperform the original methods and strong static and dynamic baselines on nearly all instances, both in total running time and worst-case update time, with speedups of up to several orders of magnitude. We further provide practical guidelines for algorithm selection and tuning. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive empirical study of heavy-light partitioning for dynamic subgraph counting, and our findings may inform other algorithms based on this technique.
item.dc:creator: Kathrin Hanauer, Sophia Heck, Monika Henzinger, Leonhard Sidl

item.title: An experimental evaluation of static k-center clustering algorithms on graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The $k$-center problem is one of the most fundamental clustering problems and has applications in a wide range of areas, including facility location, network design, data mining, and machine learning. Given a set of objects together with a distance measure, the goal is to select $k$ centers such that the maximum distance from any object to its closest center is minimized. The $k$-center problem has been studied extensively from a theoretical perspective, both in metric spaces and on graphs. While there have been experimental studies for $k$-center clustering in metric spaces, a comprehensive experimental comparison of graph-based $k$-center algorithms on large-scale graphs is still lacking. In this paper, we bridge this gap by evaluating a set of algorithms ranging from classical approaches such as Gonzalez's greedy algorithm [TCS 1985], an algorithm based on the framework established by Hochbaum and Shmoys [Math. Oper. Res. 1985], to more recent methods, including algorithms by Thorup [SICOMP 2001] and Abboud et al. [SOSA 2023]. Our study considers both running time, solution quality and the effects of parallelism on a variety of synthetic and real-world datasets. Our goal is to provide a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art $k$-center algorithms on graphs and identify the strengths and weaknesses of different approaches in practice.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Forster, Martin Gr\"osbacher

item.title: Pre-emptive Carbon Aware Scheduling for Edge Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.29945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power grids use a constantly changing mix of fossil fuels and clean renewables like solar and wind. Because of this, the {\em carbon footprint} fluctuates drastically based on time and geographic location. Time-varying carbon intensity creates opportunities to reduce carbon emissions by shifting workloads to cleaner periods, but deadlines, task dependencies, and limited edge capacity constrain this flexibility. We study carbon-aware scheduling of jobs with release times, deadlines, and arbitrary precedence constraints under piecewise-constant carbon costs. Jobs execute preemptively on a single edge server or are outsourced at job-dependent costs to an unlimited-capacity cloud, modeled as providing instantaneous execution. The objective is to minimize the sum of edge carbon costs and cloud outsourcing costs while satisfying all timing and precedence constraints. For edge-only execution, we give an exact polynomial-time algorithm. Allowing cloud outsourcing makes the problem NP-hard, but we obtain a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme through a reduction to preemptive scheduling with rejection penalties (weighted tardiness). In contrast, even two edge servers without job migration admit no polynomially bounded approximation when carbon-cost variation is unrestricted, unless \(P=NP\). We complement these theoretical results with experiments on controlled synthetic workloads and production-derived Alibaba traces. On synthetic instances, our incremental max-flow implementation is $4.96\times$ faster on average than a direct min-cost flow, while experiements on production-derived workloads evaluate its performance under realistic job structures.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Chen, Rajni Dabas, Samir Khuller, Emilie Rivkin

item.title: Approximation and Inapproximability of Non-Preemptive Dial-a-Ride
item.description: arXiv:2610.30021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The non-preemptive dial-a-ride problem (DaRP) asks for a minimum-cost route of a capacitated vehicle that serves a collection of pickup-and-delivery requests, without allowing objects to be transferred or temporarily unloaded. We study this problem and the closely related minimum-ratio Steiner $k$-Forest (S$k$F) in general symmetric metrics on $n$ locations. We develop a randomized polynomial-time algorithm with expected approximation ratio $\mathcal{O}(n^{1/4}\log^{11}n)$ for the minimum-ratio S$k$F. Our algorithm combines a deterministic approximation on hierarchically well-separated trees with randomized metric embeddings. Using this algorithm, we obtain expected $\mathcal{O}(n^{1/4}\log^{12}n)$-approximations for both the non-preemptive DaRP and the S$k$F. These guarantees improve on the previous $n^{0.3+\varepsilon}$-approximation ratios for the S$k$F and the non-preemptive DaRP, where $\varepsilon>0$ is any fixed constant. Complementing these algorithmic results, we establish the first superconstant inapproximability bounds for the non-preemptive DaRP. Under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm achieves an $x^{1/(\log\log x)^c}$-approximation for some constant $c>0$, where $x$ denotes either the number of locations $n$ or the vehicle capacity $k$. Under the quantitative Gap-ETH, we rule out every deterministic polynomial-time $x^{o(1)}$-approximation. These bounds hold even on unit-edge stars with $n=(2+o(1))k$.
item.dc:creator: Jingyang Zhao, Mingyu Xiao

item.title: Temporal Exploration and Rendezvous via Weisfeiler-Leman Colorings
item.description: arXiv:2610.30123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edge relation changes in discrete time steps. The Temporal Exploration Problem (TEXP) asks for a temporal walk that visits all vertices. We show that every connected temporal graph with $n$ vertices can be explored in $O(qn\log^3(n))$ time steps, where $q$ is the number of vertex color classes induced by the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (2-WL) coloring. For small $q$, our bound substantially improves on the known worst-case bound of $\Theta(n^2)$ in general connected temporal graphs. A corresponding walk can be constructed in deterministic polynomial time. The upper bound is complemented by lower bounds of $\Omega(n\log(n))$ when $q$ is constant and $\Omega(qn)$ when $1 \leq q \leq n$. We also apply our techniques to the Temporal Rendezvous Problem (TRP), in which two agents that do not communicate have to meet on a vertex of the temporal graph. Our exploration algorithm yields that, with only polynomial-time computational power, the agents can meet in $O(n\log^3(n))$ time steps, leaving a gap of only $\log^2(n)$ to the known lower bound. Dogeas, Erlebach, Kammer, Meintrup, and Moses Jr. [ICALP'24] have shown an $O(rn^{1+\epsilon})$ bound for TEXP, for every fixed $\epsilon > 0$, where $r$ is the number of orbits, and an $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ bound for TRP. Both results require superpolynomial computation time. Our contribution improves upon these results in several ways. First, the dependence on $n$ in the upper bounds on the number of time steps is decreased from $n^{1+\epsilon}$ to $n\log^3(n)$ for both TEXP and TRP. Second, for TEXP, we bound the number of time steps linearly by the parameter q, which is efficiently computable and upper bounded by $r$. Third, we provide novel deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for both TEXP and TRP.
item.dc:creator: Frank Kammer, Sandra Kiefer, Johannes Meintrup

item.title: De-H\"oldering factorization
item.description: arXiv:2609.07564v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a factorization notion for Lipschitz functions between metric spaces in which such a function is written as a composition of a H\"older function and a function that suitably ``undoes'' the H\"older regularity. We show simple ways to construct such ``de-H\"oldering'' factorizations. If the identity mapping on a metric space $\mathcal{M}$ admits a de-H\"oldering factorization through a metric space $\mathcal{Z}$ that has a conical geodesic bicombing, then the class of metric spaces from which one can extend $\mathcal{Z}$-valued Lipschitz functions is shown to be contained in the corresponding class of metric spaces for $\mathcal{M}$-valued Lipschitz functions. As a quick consequence of these abstract permanence properties, we deduce that every $L_1$-valued Lipschitz function from a subset of $\ell_2$ can be extended to a Lipschitz function that takes values in $L_1$ and is defined on all of $\ell_2$, answering a 1992 question of Ball. By work of Makarychev and Makarychev, this implies that every weighted graph has a vertex cut sparsifier of size $n$ and quality $O(\sqrt{\log n})$, improving Moitra's 2009 bound. We also show that for every metric space $\mathcal{Z}$ that has a conical geodesic bicombing, any metric transform of a metric space $\mathcal{M}$ has $\mathcal{Z}$-valued Lipschitz extension modulus at most a universal constant multiple of the $\mathcal{Z}$-valued Lipschitz extension modulus of $\mathcal{M}$ itself, improving the 2002 bound of Brudnyi and Shvartsman.
item.dc:creator: Assaf Naor

item.title: The Optimal Sampler for Diverse TSP Solutions: Characterization, Limits, and Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.28994v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We address the Diverse Traveling Salesman Problem (D-TSP) that seeks a set of $k$ distinct TSP tours. Each selected tour must not exceed a prescribed multiple of the optimal tour length, while the maximum pairwise Jaccard similarity within the selected set is minimized. This formulation is important for applications requiring both solution quality and fault tolerance, such as logistics planning, robotics, and strategic patrolling. We propose a novel hybrid framework that decomposes D-TSP into a sampling stage and a selection stage. The selection stage is a max-min dispersion problem, for which any approximation better than a factor of two is NP-hard; we therefore focus on the sampling stage. Our contributions are both theoretical and empirical. Theoretically, we give two end-to-end guarantees for the optimal sampling distribution, from two perspectives: including an optimal set in the sampled pool, or having at least $k$ mutually distant tours in the pool. The second reduces the number of samples from exponential to linear in $k$, at the cost of weakening the benchmark from the best $k$ tours to the best $\beta k$ for some $\beta > 1$. For practical use, we prove that a pipeline that samples spanning trees and then converts to tours does not hurt the quality of the pool in principle. Empirically, both objectives are learnable, and our experiments not only validate the analysis but also outperform the baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, by a single trained model with no fine-tuning.
item.dc:creator: Ssu-Yuan Lo, Ching-Kai Wang, Kuan-Lun Chen, Hao-Tsung Yang

item.title: Asymmetric Likelihood-Free Hypothesis Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.29798v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In likelihood-free hypothesis testing (LFHT), given samples from two unknown distributions $P,Q$ on $[n]$ with $\mathrm{d_{TV}}(P,Q)\geq\varepsilon$, and from a third distribution $D\in\{P,Q\}$, the goal is to identify whether $D=P$ or $D=Q$. We study asymmetric likelihood-free hypothesis testing, where the sample budgets $s_P$ and $s_Q$ for $P$ and $Q$ may differ, and characterize the feasible triples $(s_P,s_Q,s_D)$ up to logarithmic factors. We establish that unequal reference budgets can give a polynomial saving. For instance, for constant separation, $n$ samples from $P$ and $n^{3/4}$ from $Q$ allow testing with $\widetilde O(n^{1/4})$ samples from $D$, whereas both existing baselines---symmetric LFHT and unequal-sample closeness testing---require $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ samples from $D$. We further apply our results to non-adaptive distribution 2-clustering, where the sample allocation among $k$ distributions must be fixed before observing any data. We obtain matching upper and lower bounds for this problem up to logarithmic factors in terms of the domain size, number of distributions, smaller cluster size, and separation, both with one cluster distribution known and with both unknown. Comparing with known bounds for adaptive sample allocation gives a worst-case adaptivity gap of $\widetilde\Theta(k^{1/4})$.
item.dc:creator: Gunjan Kumar, Yash Pote, Jonathan Scarlett

item.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
item.description: arXiv:2610.29898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$. For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.
item.dc:creator: Shihao Shao, Dacheng Tao

item.title: Disjoint Stable Matchings in Linear Time
item.description: arXiv:2011.13248v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that given a SM instance G as input we can find a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in time linear in the input size. This extends two classical results: 1. The Gale-Shapley algorithm, which can find at most two ("extreme") pairwise edge-disjoint stable matchings of G in linear time, and 2. The polynomial-time algorithm for finding a largest collection of pairwise edge-disjoint perfect matchings (without the stability requirement) in a bipartite graph, obtained by combining K\"{o}nig's characterization with Tutte's f-factor algorithm. Moreover, we also give an algorithm to enumerate all maximum-length chains of disjoint stable matchings in the lattice of stable matchings of a given instance. This algorithm takes time polynomial in the input size for enumerating each chain. We also derive the expected number of such chains in a random instance of Stable Matching. For the Stable Roomates problem, we show that determining if a given instance admits at most two disjoint stable matchings or three disjoint stable matchings is NP-complete.
item.dc:creator: Aadityan Ganesh, Vishwa Prakash HV, Prajakta Nimbhorkar, Geevarghese Philip

item.title: Dynamic k-center clustering with lifetimes
item.description: arXiv:2603.23348v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The $k$-center problem is a fundamental clustering variant with applications in learning systems and data summarization. In several real-world scenarios, the dataset to be clustered is not static, but evolves over time, as new data points arrive and old ones become stale. To account for dynamicity, the $k$-center problem has been mainly studied under the sliding window setting, where only the $N$ most recent points are considered non-stale, or the fully dynamic setting, where arbitrary sequences of point arrivals and deletions without prior notice may occur. In this paper, we introduce the dynamic setting with lifetimes, which bridges the two aforementioned classical settings by still allowing arbitrary arrivals and deletions, but making the deletion time of each point known upon its arrival. Under this new setting, we devise a deterministic $(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm with $\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)$ amortized update time and memory usage linear in the number of currently active points. Moreover, we develop a deterministic $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that, under tame update sequences, has $\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)$ worst-case update time and heavily sublinear working memory.
item.dc:creator: Simone Moretti, Paolo Pellizzoni, Andrea Pietracaprina, Geppino Pucci

item.title: The Binary Tree Mechanism is Optimal for Differentially Private Continual Counting
item.description: arXiv:2607.00876v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Private continual counting is a fundamental problem in differential privacy: given a binary stream of length $n$, where each $1$ corresponds to the contribution of one individual, the goal is to release all running counts while protecting the privacy of each individual. For fixed privacy parameters, the standard binary tree mechanism achieves expected $\ell_\infty$ error $O(\log^{3/2} n)$ under approximate differential privacy and $O(\log^2 n)$ under pure differential privacy. Whether these dependences on the stream length are necessary has remained a central open problem. For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, we prove a lower bound of $\Omega(\log^{3/2} n)$ under approximate DP with sufficiently small fixed $\delta>0$, and a lower bound of $\Omega(\log^2 n)$ under pure DP. These bounds establish the optimality of the binary tree mechanism in both settings. The bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Both proofs use the same decomposition and accumulation of residual noise along a tree. As a consequence of the approximate-DP bound, we also obtain a largest-possible separation between hereditary discrepancy and private $\ell_\infty$ error for linear queries, showing that the known general upper bound in terms of hereditary discrepancy has the optimal dependence on the number of queries.
item.dc:creator: Konstantina Bairaktari, Markus Engelund Dahl, Kasper Green Larsen

item.title: On the Assadi Liu Tarjan Auction Algorithm for Bipartite Matching: Simplification, Alternative Analysis, and Hard Instance
item.description: arXiv:2607.07439v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan [SOSA'21] gave an auction algorithm that outputs a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximation to Maximum Matching in bipartite graphs. Their algorithm computes a sequence of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ maximal matchings in subgraphs of the input graph and can be implemented in the multi-pass streaming setting with $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ passes in a straightforward manner, which constitutes the state-of-the-art pass/approximation trade-off result in the multi-pass streaming setting. Their analysis uses tools from combinatorial auctions and, at its heart, relies on a clever potential function argument. Their proof, however, provides only limited insight into the inner workings of the algorithm. In this paper, we revisit the ALT-algorithm and present the following contributions. Simplification: The ALT-algorithm is built upon a freezing mechanism where vertices on one side of the bipartition that have already been rematched $\Theta(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ times over the course of the algorithm remain matched to their current partner forever. We show that this mechanism is in fact unnecessary, i.e., no special treatment of such vertices is needed. Alternative Analysis: We give an alternative analysis of the algorithm that is based on augmenting paths. Our analysis allows for a reinterpretation as one that follows the traditional approach of searching for and eliminating augmenting paths. Our analysis also copes with the removal of the freezing mechanism in a natural way, whereas the analysis of Assadi et al. strictly depends on its use. Hard Instance: We provide the first hard instance on which the algorithm requires $\Omega(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ iterations/maximal matching computations. The instance is a simple path graph, where we exhibit a cyclic behaviour that prevents fast progress.
item.dc:creator: Christian Konrad, Kheeran K. Naidu, Archie Walton, Eric Wang

item.title: A minimum witness for the 3/2 configuration-linear-program gap in two-weight graph balancing, unique at its size
item.description: arXiv:2608.13318v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Restricted assignment minimizes makespan, the busiest machine's load, when each job has one size and a set of allowed machines. Its tightest studied relaxation is the configuration linear program, which fractionally gives each machine whole job sets that fit. Its integrality gap, the worst-case ratio of integral optimum to relaxation value, is open in general. On two-weight graph balancing (sizes 1 and 2, each job allowed on at most two machines) the gap is known: Jansen, Land, and Maack (2016) give both bounds. Their Table 1 instance attains 3/2, and their Corollary 11 bound of 2-s/b for sizes s < b matches it at {1,2}. We ask how small such an instance, a witness, can be. We give a six-job witness I* on the complete graph on four machines: unit jobs form a cycle through all four, and two weight-2 jobs take the remaining edges. I* has integral optimum 3 against relaxation value 2, one job fewer than the smallest earlier witness of this class. We prove I* minimum and unique at its size, on any number of machines: no instance with at most five jobs reaches gap 3/2, and at six jobs I* is the only witness, up to relabeling machines and adding unusable machines. At seven jobs uniqueness fails: we classify all thirteen witnesses, including the Jansen-Land-Maack instance. Eight jobs give 154, nine 1,662. At least four machines are necessary. Kartak et al. (2015) classified the extremal non-round-up instances of the same relaxation in one-dimensional cutting stock for small demand; the Discussion relates them. Recognizing witnesses at relaxation value 2, shared by all ours, is coNP-complete, so no min-max characterization with polynomially checkable conditions exists unless NP = coNP. Every feasibility decision behind the exhaustive claims was made twice, in floating-point and exact rational arithmetic, with identical results. We accept the pipeline's negatives only after it rediscovers I*.
item.dc:creator: Adam Y. Shavit

item.title: The 11/6 supremum of the Wang-Sitters rounding scheme for graph balancing
item.description: arXiv:2609.03890v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wang and Sitters' 11/6-approximation for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) is not one algorithm but a set of permitted executions. Step 1 may return any feasible solution of the fractional relaxation. Step 3 may match remaining jobs to the rounding's slots in many ways. We determine exactly what that latitude permits: ratios arbitrarily close to 11/6, none reaching it, so 11/6 is the least constant bounding every permitted run. We then determine the worst-case guarantee, against the optimum itself, as a function of the big-job threshold beta, the fractional share at or above which Step 2 assigns a job. On Wang and Sitters' own range 1/2 < beta < 1 the guarantee is exactly max{3/2 + beta/2, 5/2 - beta}. We extend the same eligibility rule to 0 < beta <= 1/2, outside the range they state. There a big job's two shares can both reach the threshold, so Step 2 acquires a third choice. We determine it too: exactly 3/2 + (1-beta)floor(1/beta), hence unbounded as beta falls. The worst-case ratio is therefore known at every threshold in (0,1), and attained at none. Consequently 2/3 is the unique optimal threshold, and the guarantee jumps at one half and again at every threshold 1/k below it, rather than degrading smoothly. A companion note examines changes that leave the constant unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Adam Y. Shavit (Hunter College,The Graduate Center, CUNY)

item.title: Minimum-makespan completion and vertex selection leave the Wang-Sitters constant at 11/6
item.description: arXiv:2609.10004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Wang and Sitters' rounding scheme for graph balancing (each job allowed on at most two machines) keeps the makespan, the busiest machine's load, within 11/6 of the optimum, and a companion note shows that no smaller constant holds. One suspected cause is Step 3's freedom to match leftover jobs to slots in any valid way. We show that removing that freedom does not improve the constant. An idealized oracle that always picks the valid matching with the smallest makespan still has worst-case constant exactly 11/6 against the optimum. Both natural 7/4 bounds for it, against the relaxation's target and against the optimum, are false. Requiring Step 1 to return a vertex (corner) of the relaxation does not help when that vertex is chosen adversarially. The loss therefore does not come from Step 3's freedom alone. We also prove a reduction confining every overload above 7/4 to two shapes, give a seven-machine instance on which the natural two-phase repair fails, and prove a strict 7/4 bound on the generalized three-path family.
item.dc:creator: Adam Y. Shavit (Hunter College,The Graduate Center, CUNY)

item.title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.27216v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $\alpha_{GW}+\tilde{\Omega}(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $\alpha_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/\sqrt{d})$. Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm \epsilon$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.
item.dc:creator: Rares-Darius Buhai, Suprovat Ghoshal, Neng Huang, Pravesh Kothari, Euiwoong Lee, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev

item.title: The Limits of Post-Selection Generalization
item.description: arXiv:1806.06100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While statistics and machine learning offer numerous methods for ensuring generalization, these methods often fail in the presence of adaptivity---the common practice in which the choice of analysis depends on previous interactions with the same dataset. A recent line of work has introduced powerful, general purpose algorithms that ensure post hoc generalization (also called robust or post-selection generalization), which says that, given the output of the algorithm, it is hard to find any statistic for which the data differs significantly from the population it came from. In this work we show several limitations on the power of algorithms satisfying post hoc generalization. First, we show a tight lower bound on the error of any algorithm that satisfies post hoc generalization and answers adaptively chosen statistical queries, showing a strong barrier to progress in post selection data analysis. Second, we show that post hoc generalization is not closed under composition, despite many examples of such algorithms exhibiting strong composition properties.
item.dc:creator: Kobbi Nissim, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Uri Stemmer, Jonathan Ullman

item.title: Engineering Scalable Distributed List Ranking
item.description: arXiv:2606.09318v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The list ranking problem is one of the classical problems of parallel computing, with nontrivial algorithms and many applications as a subroutine for solving other problems. While it has been intensively studied in the early days of parallel computing, few things happened in the last 20 years. In particular, there is little work on scaling list ranking to large machines and input sizes. We reconsider list ranking starting from the ground-breaking results of Sibeyn a quarter century ago. We employ algorithm and performance engineering to improve his sparse ruling-set algorithm, making it capable of scaling to many processors, and provide a more detailed analysis of the impact of the algorithm's parameters, further guiding our practical implementation. We perform an extensive experimental study across a variety of input instances with different structural properties. We demonstrate that indirect communication, exploiting input locality, and message coalescing allows scaling to billions of elements on up to 24,576 cores.

item.title: Moment Ambiguity and the Limits of Robust Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2609.31090v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study fundamental information-theoretic limits of robust stochastic optimization when the distribution is known only through its exact moment sequence. We develop a unified framework that produces families of distinct distributions sharing all moments yet inducing radically different optimal decisions, thereby establishing strong impossibility results for a range of decision problems under moment ambiguity. Our binary and $N$-way moment-matching constructions separate quantiles, threshold regions, and online selection opportunities while preserving every moment. For the newsvendor problem, moment equivalence causes quantile ambiguity, inducing any fixed or randomized order quantity to fail arbitrarily badly. For revenue maximization, no deterministic or randomized posted pricing scheme can secure a nontrivial approximation relative to the full-information benchmark. For the secretary problem with cardinal observations, the optimal robust success probability under exact moment disclosure is the classical finite-horizon value $s_m$, even for i.i.d. observations. This value converges to $1/e$, compared with the full-information limit of approximately $0.5801$ due to Gilbert and Mosteller (J. Am. Stat. Assoc., 1966). We also recover and expand upon the recent impossibility result of Correa et al. (STOC, 2026) for prophet inequalities with moment knowledge. For every fixed $r\ge1$, exact moment knowledge can yield at best a $\Theta(1/\log m)$ competitive ratio, even when competing against relaxed benchmarks based on expected $r$-th order statistics or when the algorithm is allowed to select $r$ items.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Cristi, Matteo Russo, Jiechen Zhang

item.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
item.description: arXiv:2610.28141v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.
item.dc:creator: Ioannis Anagnostides, Constantinos Daskalakis, Gabriele Farina, Noah Golowich, Tuomas Sandholm, Brian Hu Zhang
